newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: FORECAST-Analysts revise up BHP's profit.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-Analysts revise up BHP's profit.

text.p: Share analysts have revised up their profit forecasts for Australia's biggest company, The Broken Hill Pty Co Ltd (BHP), after the embattled blue chip this week announced a strong rise in copper production.
The revisions put the steel-making and resources giant on track for a slightly higher annual net profit of between A$1.35 billion and A$1.4 billion before abnormal items.
The result for the year ended May 31, to be reported on June 27, would mark a return to growth in pre-abnormal annual profit for BHP, after 1995/96 profit fell 20 percent to A$1.29 billion.

BHP has been savaged by the share market at times over the past 12 months, as the group comes to grips with underperforming assets, an elusive bull market for commodities and the effect of low inflation on earnings growth.
Investors last attacked BHP's share price in late May, after it warned of flat earnings until late calendar 1998 and said trading conditions remained tough. Profit forecasts tumbled.
But some share analysts again refined forecasts after BHP released strong monthly and annual production data on Tuesday.
BHP reported a 19 percent surge in production of copper concentrates and a strong rise in steel dispatches in May.
The higher copper output follows a rally in cash copper prices after the Sumitomo trading scandal of mid-1996.
"It was a good production report," one analyst told Reuters.
Another analyst said he was also revising up his current 1996/97 profit forecast of A$1.325 billion. "It will probably go up a little bit to the A$1.35 billion mark," he said.
Fund manager Warren Edney, of Colonial Investment Management, sees net profit before abnormals of A$1.4 billion.
"It (the copper price) has been quite high and it has held up pretty strongly in May, so that might make a bit of a difference," Edney said.
A substantial amount of copper concentrate sold toward the end of 1996/97 has not yet been priced, and an estimate based on the prevailing price is used in BHP's final accounts.
Another fund manager declined to give a forecast for 1996/97 but said BHP might surprise analysts in future years after puncturing their forecasts with May's profit warning.
"They have pitched the expectations at a very low level," he said. "I find it hard to believe things are as bad as they have painted."
"Recent developments are going to add to that upside surprise," he added, citing a weaker Australian dollar and a rally in copper prices.
BHP says its after-tax profit is boosted A$35 million by every one U.S. cent fall in the Australian dollar.
The outlook for BHP's earnings are mixed, with some analysts still bullish on the copper price, though the London Metals Exchange three-month price is trading below spot.
"The share price at the moment is starting to heat up to the levels that certainly fully factor in the current year's earnings of around that A$1.9 billion mark," an analyst said.
"If copper collapses you will see the share price collapse as well."
BHP shares closed on Wednesday at A$19.27, well above the depths of late 1996, when the stock sank beneath A$16.
BHP has hinted it will take more asset write-downs as abnormal losses in its 1996/97 results, but analysts contacted by Reuters would not speculate on the size of the losses.
BHP has already written off the value of its huge Newcastle steelworks north of Sydney and disposed of its stake in the Dai Hung oil field off Vietnam, which proved to be a disappointment.
BHP says all its assets are under review.
BHP is expected to pay a steady final dividend of 26 cents for the second half-year, according to a survey of brokerages by Barceps forecasting service.
BHP paid 25 cents for the first half and 51 cents in total for 1995/96.
-- Melbourne bureau 6713-9286-1421
